title: Catching the London off Guard With QB6!! | The Sensei Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We're Black, and against d4 out comes the knight to f6 — let's go.
The bishop to f4 — the London System, one of White's most popular setups.
We're going to test our opponent on a London line I've used myself, one a lot of people still don't know. It starts with c5, hitting the center immediately.
White props things up with e3.
We take on d4, forcing the issue.
After White recaptures, we quickly fire off the queen to b6 — the very tricky line, and inexperienced London players hate it because it hits both b2 and d4.

He plays the knight to c3. If you know the first thing about this line you don't rush that — the theoretically good try for White is different, something Rosen has analyzed — but a natural developer reaches for the knight to c3.

And here's the point: we play d6, deliberately luring that knight to stay on c3. London players do not like having their knight committed to c3 — it clogs the natural pawn setup London players lean on.
White shores up b2 with the rook to b1.
Now the fianchetto should feel natural: g6. If you play e6 instead you block in your own light-squared bishop, so we let it breathe on the long diagonal.
White brings out the knight to f3; we complete the fianchetto with the bishop to g7.
White develops the bishop to e2; we castle.
White castles too — a normal-looking middlegame, but our queen sortie has already made White slightly uncomfortable.

There are a couple of viable setups. One is to trade this bishop for White's knight and then post the knight on c6 pressuring d4 — but I don't love parting with the bishop, so I play the bishop to f5, eyeing c2.
White plays h3. A tempting move here is the knight to h4, but that's succumbing to one-move-itis — chasing a single idea while ignoring the rest of the board.
We develop the knight to c6, piling onto d4.
White lashes out with d5 — a committal push London players usually dislike, but he goes for it, kicking our knight.
The knight jumps into b4 — and this is the whole point of the bishop on f5: together they gang up on c2 and win a tempo.
White defends with the knight back to e1, an ugly, passive square. Most players in the 1700-1800 range would shuffle the rook toward c1, which is even more passive.
We bring the rook to c8, stacking up on the c-file.
White plays a3, poking our knight on b4.

We retreat the knight to a6, planning to redeploy it to c5 — and one point I want to make through this game is that people become terrified of a move like the knight to a6 when there's no reason to fear it.
White develops the bishop to e3, hitting our queen.
We slide the queen to a5 — and honestly this drops a pawn; I completely forgot it was hanging. I should have brought the other rook over instead, a clean improving move rather than this.
Rewinding to that moment: the rook belonged on c8, keeping everything defended — I simply overlooked that the pawn was hanging and gave it away for no reason.
